AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: there are no specific criteria for a step-down or withdrawal dose of omalizumab. Our purpose was to evaluate the viability of a protocol for OMAlizumab DOse REduction (the OMADORE study) in severe allergic asthma (SAA).

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: the study population included 35 SAA patients treated during a minimum period of one year with oral corticosteroids (OC) equivalent to a mean daily dose of 4 mg of methyl-prednisolone. To qualify for the protocol, the patients had to have received treatment with OMA ≥ one year and a half, OC dose had to have reached the lowest tolerated dose and spirometry had to be ≥ at entry.

AbstractText.Label: INTERVENTION
AbstractText.content: a) OMA dose was reduced by half; b) if patients were clinically stable after 6 months, the dose was halved again; c) if repeated OC boosters were needed and/or spirometry worsened ≥ 10%, OMA dose was raised to the previous figure until stabilization.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Mean age was 52.5 (17) years, median monthly OC dose was 120 (IQR: 225) mg. Pulmonary function: FVC: 79.7 (20.2)%; FEV1 : 64.8 (21.7)%; FEV1 / FVC: 61.7(13.8)%. OMA could be withdrawn in 34.3% of the patients; 22.9% tolerated a reduction, and in 42.9% the dose could not be modified. Follow-up time after reduction or withdrawal ranged from 12 to 30 months. There were no severe exacerbations requiring emergency assistance or admission.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: The OMADORE study found that in more than 50% of SAA patients on OC, OMA dose can be safely reduced or withdrawn based on a progressive dose reduction protocol.
